Baby & Child

6 Month Old Milestones: What Babies Do by 6 Months

Updated: August 26, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

By 6 months, most babies know familiar people, laugh, take turns making sounds, roll from tummy to back, push up on straight arms, reach for toys they want, and explore objects with their mouth. These come from the CDC milestone checklist, which describes skills at least 75 percent of babies show by this age. This guide walks through the half-year snapshot: social, language, movement, feeding, and sleep, plus the signs that are worth a call to your pediatrician. Every baby moves through this list at their own pace, so treat it as a map, not a scorecard.

Social and language skills: laughter, squeals, and turn-taking

Milestone checklists describe what most babies can do by a given age, not what every baby must do on schedule. The CDC list was revised in 2022 to set each milestone at the age when at least 75 percent of babies show the skill, a deliberate shift from older lists built on 50 percent averages, so a listed skill is one most babies already have. On the social side, the 6-month list includes knowing familiar people, enjoying looking at themselves in a mirror, and laughing. Your baby may light up when you walk in, study your face during feeds, and react differently to a stranger than to a grandparent they see every week. If a few items have not appeared yet, that alone is not a verdict. Babies develop along a range, and the half-year mark is a snapshot, not a test.

Language at this age sounds like a conversation without words. Most 6 month olds take turns making sounds with you: you speak, they answer with a coo or a squeal, and back and forth it goes. Blowing raspberries and squealing are normal, and they are useful practice for the mouth muscles that speech will need later. You can help without any special program. Talk through what you are doing, pause so your baby can reply, and copy their sounds back. Narrating a diaper change counts. So does singing badly in the kitchen. The amount of everyday back and forth matters far more than flashcards or apps.

Movement: rolling, pushing up, and steadier sitting

By 6 months, most babies roll from tummy to back, and many are starting to roll from back to tummy as well. During tummy time, expect your baby to push up on straight arms and hold their chest high off the floor. When you place them sitting, many will lean forward on their hands in a tripod position rather than sitting steadily alone. Independent sitting usually firms up over the following months. We cover the full rolling and sitting timelines in separate guides, so here the point is simply the checklist expectation: rolling at least one direction and pushing up on straight arms are typical by now.

Hands are busy at this age. Most 6 month olds reach out to grab a toy they want, bring objects toward their mouth, and explore almost everything by mouthing it. That gumming and licking is not a bad habit. It is how babies gather information about texture, shape, and temperature. Practical safety follows from these new skills. Never leave your baby unattended on a bed, couch, or changing table, because a roll can happen in a second. Keep coins, button batteries, and anything small enough to swallow out of reach, and offer sturdy toys with no loose parts that can break off.

Feeding at 6 months: milk still leads, solids begin

Around 6 months is when the AAP and WHO point to starting solid foods, alongside breast milk or formula rather than instead of it. Milk remains the main source of nutrition through the rest of the first year, so early solids are about practice, taste, and texture more than calories. Whether your baby is ready depends on skills, not the date on the calendar, and our starting solids guide walks through those readiness signs, first foods, and the puree versus baby-led question in detail, and a separate guide covers introducing allergens like peanut and egg one at a time.

A typical day still revolves around milk. Many 6 month olds take a breast or bottle feed every 3 to 4 hours while awake, with one or two small solid sessions tucked in when the baby is rested and mildly hungry rather than starving. Follow your baby's signals instead of a strict clock. Leaning in with an open mouth means more. Closing the lips, turning the head, or pushing food away means done, and by 6 months most babies can tell you this clearly. Respecting those signals now builds a trust in mealtimes that pays off well into the toddler years.

Sleep at 6 months: totals and naps

Most 6 month olds sleep about 12 to 16 hours in every 24 hours, counting naps, which matches the range pediatric sleep guidance gives for babies between 4 and 12 months. Two to three naps a day is typical at this age, often a morning nap, an early afternoon nap, and sometimes a short late catnap that fades over the coming months. Night stretches are usually longer than they were at 3 months, but plenty of healthy 6 month olds still wake to feed. If night waking is your main question, our guide on sleeping through the night covers that stage in detail.

You can support sleep without a complicated system. A short, repeatable wind-down helps: a feed, a fresh diaper, a song or a book, then into the crib drowsy. Keep the room dark and boring during night feeds so they stay brief. Safe sleep still applies at this age: place your baby on their back on a firm, flat surface, in their own crib or bassinet, with no blankets, pillows, bumpers, or soft toys. A baby who rolls both ways can be left in whatever position they settle into, but you should still start every sleep on the back.

Play ideas, red flags, and the 6-month checkup

Play at 6 months can be simple and repetitive, because repetition is exactly what a learning brain wants. Take turns making sounds and copy your baby's noises back. Play peekaboo with your hands or a light cloth. Offer a baby-safe mirror and watch them study the face inside it. Give washable toys they can mouth freely, and rotate a few favorites rather than piling up many. Daily floor time on a clean blanket gives rolling and reaching room to grow. Reading aloud counts at any age, because your baby is absorbing rhythm and tone long before they understand a single word.

Bring your questions to the 6-month checkup, where your pediatrician will measure growth, ask about milestones, feeding, and sleep, and give any vaccines due on the schedule. Call sooner if your baby shows no affection for familiar caregivers, makes no vowel sounds, does not roll in either direction, does not reach for things, seems very stiff or very floppy, or loses skills they once had. None of these is a diagnosis on its own, but each deserves a professional look, and early support helps most when it starts early. It can help to note dates and questions in BeMama or on paper as they occur to you, so the visit covers what matters most.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC milestones describe skills that most children can do by a particular age across social, language, thinking, and movement domains. They support observation and conversation but do not replace standardized developmental screening.

Individual skills vary, but caregiver concern matters. Missing several expected skills, losing a skill, or a difference in movement, communication, hearing, or vision should be discussed promptly.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to preserve dated observations, growth, activities, and questions for well-child visits. It cannot label development as normal or delayed.

When to seek help

Contact your child’s healthcare professional whenever you are concerned or notice loss of a skill. Seek urgent care for an acute change, breathing difficulty, loss of responsiveness, or seizure-like activity.

Evidence notes updated: August 5, 2026

Key takeaways

  • By 6 months most babies know familiar people, laugh, and take turns making sounds with you.
  • Rolling from tummy to back, pushing up on straight arms, and leaning on hands to sit are typical movement skills.
  • Solids usually start around 6 months while breast milk or formula remains the main nutrition.
  • Expect about 12 to 16 hours of total sleep in 24 hours, usually with 2 to 3 naps.
  • Call your pediatrician if your baby is not rolling either direction, not reaching, makes no vowel sounds, shows no affection, or loses skills.

Frequently asked questions

What should a 6 month old be doing?

By 6 months, most babies know familiar people, laugh, take turns making sounds, blow raspberries, roll from tummy to back, push up on straight arms, reach for toys, and mouth objects to explore them. Many also lean on their hands when placed sitting and close their lips to show they do not want more food. Babies vary, so a missing item is a reason to watch and mention it at the checkup, not a reason to panic.

When do babies babble?

Many babies start making vowel sounds like ah and eh by around 4 to 6 months, and turn-taking sound games are typical at 6 months. Consonant babbling such as bababa or mamama often follows between about 6 and 9 months. If your baby makes no vowel sounds at all by 6 months, mention it to your pediatrician.

How much should a 6 month old sleep?

Most 6 month olds sleep about 12 to 16 hours in every 24 hours, including naps. Two to three naps a day is typical, and many healthy babies this age still wake at night to feed. Talk with your pediatrician if your baby consistently sleeps far outside that range or seems exhausted despite normal totals.

What happens at the 6 month checkup?

At the 6-month checkup, your pediatrician measures weight, length, and head size, asks about milestones, feeding, and sleep, and gives any vaccines due on the schedule. It is a natural moment to raise concerns about rolling, reaching, sounds, or lost skills. Bring your questions written down, because these visits go quickly.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
